docs.title: Agentic AI & Multi Agent Systems
docs.text: Single- and multi-agent systems that plan, call tools, coordinate steps and operate within defined controls, with autonomy introduced as an engineered decision.

docs.title: Planning and task decomposition
docs.text: Turning an instruction into an ordered set of steps the system can actually carry out, with the plan visible and inspectable rather than implied by whatever the model felt like doing.

docs.title: Tool use and system access
docs.text: The functions, queries and APIs an agent may call, what arguments it may pass, and the explicit list of things it may not touch. The boundary is the design.

docs.title: Multi-agent coordination
docs.text: Where a task genuinely splits into research, drafting, checking and execution, agents with distinct responsibilities and a defined protocol between them, rather than one prompt pretending to be a team.

docs.title: State, memory and recovery
docs.text: What the system remembers within a task and across tasks, and what it does when a step fails halfway through. Recovery design is most of the engineering.

docs.title: Human approval points
docs.text: The moments where the run stops and a person decides. Placed where the consequence is material, not where they are least inconvenient.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text: Every step, tool call, input and decision recorded, so an outcome can be explained afterwards to a customer, an auditor or a court.

docs.title: Suggest
docs.text: The system proposes; a person does the work. Nothing changes without a human action. The right place to start with almost anything.

docs.title: Draft for approval
docs.text: The system produces the output and a person approves or edits it before it leaves the building. Most production value sits here.

docs.title: Act within bounds
docs.text: The system executes inside a narrow, reversible envelope, escalating anything outside it. Requires evaluation evidence before it is granted.

docs.title: Act and report
docs.text: The system runs and a person reviews after the fact. Justified only by measured performance over time on a task where a mistake is recoverable.

docs.title: What an agentic build actually consists of
docs.text: Very little of it is prompt writing. The engineering lives in what the system may reach, what it does when a step fails, and how the run is reconstructed afterwards.

docs.title: Four steps, and you have to earn each one
docs.text: A system moves up only on evidence from its own evaluation results. Nothing here is granted because a demonstration went well.

docs.title: What is a multi-agent system, in practical terms?
docs.text: A design in which distinct components each hold a defined responsibility, for example gathering information, drafting, checking and executing, and communicate through a defined protocol. It is worth the extra complexity only where the task genuinely splits along those lines. Where it does not, a single agent, or a deterministic workflow with one model call in it, is cheaper, faster and easier to audit.

docs.title: How do you decide how much autonomy an agent should have?
docs.text: Autonomy is treated as an engineered control decision rather than a selling point. Human oversight is the default wherever a decision is material. More autonomous operation is introduced only where the workflow, the risk level and measured evaluation evidence justify it, in defined steps: suggest, draft for approval, act within bounds, then act and report.

docs.title: How do you stop an agent doing something it should not?
docs.text: By constraining what it can reach rather than by asking it nicely. The tools, queries and APIs available to an agent are an explicit allow-list, arguments are validated, irreversible actions are gated behind human approval, and every step and tool call is recorded so the run can be reconstructed afterwards.

docs.title: Entitlement-aware retrieval
docs.text: The hard part of enterprise AI is not retrieval, it is retrieval that respects who is allowed to see what. We model permissions first and index second.

docs.title: Context and semantic layers
docs.text: A stable vocabulary between your systems and the model, so the answer does not change because someone renamed a column.

docs.title: MCP integration to systems of record
docs.text: CRM, ERP, case management, document stores and internal APIs. MCP has won as a connector standard; the unsolved parts are identity, audit and gateway policy, which is where the work is.

docs.title: Evaluation and observability
docs.text: Instrumented from day one on open standards, so you are never locked into whoever is monitoring you. This is also what makes the run contract possible.

docs.title: Lineage and provenance
docs.text: Where an answer came from, which documents, which version, at what time. Your auditor will ask, and so will your customer.

docs.title: Legacy enablement
docs.text: Long-lived systems that resist change. AI coding gains are large on greenfield and close to nothing on complex legacy, which is precisely why this stays human work.

docs.title: What is the biggest barrier to getting value from enterprise AI?
docs.text: Data readiness and access, not model capability. 58% name data readiness and access as their number one barrier (KPMG 2026), 72% cite data quality as the top obstacle (Deloitte Private 2026), and three in four UK professional services firms are unready on data, orchestration and monitoring (GOV.UK 2026).

docs.title: What is entitlement-aware retrieval?
docs.text: Retrieval that respects who is allowed to see what. Permissions are modelled first and the index is built second, so a model can reach the information it needs and nothing it should not. It is the part of enterprise RAG that most often stops a rollout.

docs.title: Do you use MCP to connect to systems of record?
docs.text: Yes. MCP has effectively won as a connector standard for CRM, ERP, case management, document stores and internal APIs. The unsolved parts are identity, audit and gateway policy, which is where the engineering work actually sits.

docs.title: AI Evaluation & Observability
docs.text: Golden datasets graded pass or fail, judges calibrated against human labels, regression checks, and drift detection including judge drift.

docs.title: Golden datasets
docs.text: A maintained set of at least 100 labelled examples per system, built from real cases rather than invented ones, and versioned alongside the code that is graded against it.

docs.title: Pass or fail, not one to five
docs.text: Binary grading against an agreed definition of correct. A five-point scale hides disagreement inside the middle three points and makes a regression impossible to detect.

docs.title: Judge calibration
docs.text: Where a model does the grading, it is calibrated against human labels before it is relied on, and re-calibrated on a schedule. An uncalibrated judge is an opinion with a number attached.

docs.title: Regression checks on every release
docs.text: The suite runs before a change ships. Below the acceptance threshold means it does not ship, and that threshold is agreed before the build rather than negotiated after it.

docs.title: Drift detection, including judge drift
docs.text: Input distribution drift, silent model version changes by a supplier, and movement in the evaluator’s own behaviour. The third is the one most teams never watch.

docs.title: Open standards throughout
docs.text: Instrumented on open standards from day one, so you are never locked into whoever happens to be monitoring you, and can take the measurement with you.

docs.title: How we measure an AI system
docs.text: The same approach on every engagement, published so you can check it before you buy anything.

docs.title: Why grade AI output pass or fail rather than on a one-to-five scale?
docs.text: Because a five-point scale hides disagreement inside the middle three points, which makes regressions impossible to detect reliably. Binary grading against an agreed definition of correct forces the definition to be written down, and makes a change in quality visible the moment it happens.

docs.title: What is judge drift and why does it matter?
docs.text: Judge drift is movement in the behaviour of the model doing the grading, as opposed to drift in the input data or a silent version change by a supplier. It matters because it silently invalidates your quality measurements: the system looks stable while the instrument measuring it has moved.

docs.title: When should evaluation be built into an AI system?
docs.text: At the start. Evaluation designed in from day one is what makes an acceptance threshold enforceable and a support-and-run contract possible. Evaluation bolted on after an incident can only tell you what is happening now, not what changed.

docs.title: NLP, Speech & Vision
docs.text: Extraction, classification, sentiment, speech and image or video intelligence, built where the use case supports it and graded against a definition of correct.

docs.title: Document extraction
docs.text: Pulling structured fields out of invoices, forms, contracts, statements and correspondence, including the scanned, rotated and photographed versions that arrive in real post rooms.

docs.title: Classification and routing
docs.text: Deciding what a message, case or document is and where it should go. Usually the highest-value language task in a business, and the least glamorous.

docs.title: Sentiment and theme analysis
docs.text: What customers are actually saying across reviews, tickets and calls, aggregated into themes a team can act on rather than a single number nobody acts on.

docs.title: Speech to text and voice interfaces
docs.text: Transcription, diarisation, call summarisation and voice-driven interaction, with accent and audio-quality performance measured on your recordings rather than a vendor benchmark.

docs.title: Image and video intelligence
docs.text: Detection, classification, condition assessment and quality checking, where the visual task is defined tightly enough for a consistent answer to exist.

docs.title: Multilingual handling
docs.text: Detection, translation and language-specific behaviour, with the accuracy stated per language instead of averaged into a flattering headline.

docs.title: Define correct first
docs.text: Two people labelling the same hundred documents will disagree. Where they disagree, no system can be graded, so the definition is settled before the build.

docs.title: Confidence drives routing
docs.text: High-confidence output flows through; low-confidence output goes to a person. That threshold is the main control you have, and it is yours to set.

docs.title: Measured on your material
docs.text: Performance on a public benchmark tells you very little about performance on your forms, your accents and your photographs.

docs.title: Accuracy stated per class
docs.text: An overall figure hides the category that matters. We report per class, including the rare ones, because that is where the cost of an error usually lives.

docs.title: What language, speech and vision work do you take on?
docs.text: Document extraction, classification and routing, sentiment and theme analysis, speech to text with diarisation and summarisation, image and video intelligence, and multilingual handling. The qualifier that matters is whether the use case supports it: the task has to be defined tightly enough that a consistent correct answer exists.

docs.title: How accurate will an extraction or classification system be?
docs.text: That cannot honestly be answered before it is measured on your own material, because performance on public benchmarks says little about performance on your forms, accents and photographs. The engagement establishes accuracy per class against a labelled set built from real cases, and the confidence threshold that routes uncertain output to a person is set from those results.

docs.title: What happens to the cases the system is unsure about?
docs.text: They go to a person. Confidence-based routing is the primary control in this category: high-confidence output flows through, low-confidence output is queued for human review with the reason attached, and the volume in that queue is reported so the threshold can be tuned deliberately rather than discovered.

docs.title: LLM Integration & RAG
docs.text: Add model intelligence to existing products and knowledge environments with retrieval, permissions and grounded context, rather than a chat box bolted to the side.

docs.title: Retrieval over your own content
docs.text: Documents, records, tickets, policies and the knowledge that currently lives in three systems and one person’s head. Chunking, indexing and ranking designed around how the content is actually written.

docs.title: Permissions and entitlements
docs.text: Retrieval that respects who is allowed to see what. Permissions are modelled first and the index is built second, because a model that can reach everything is a data-protection incident waiting for a prompt.

docs.title: Grounded answers with citations
docs.text: Output tied to the source passages it came from, so a reader can check it. Ungrounded fluency is the single most expensive failure mode in this category.

docs.title: Context and prompt engineering
docs.text: What goes into the window, in what order, at what cost, with the assembly written as code that can be tested rather than a string somebody edits in production.

docs.title: Model selection, routing and fallback
docs.text: Which model handles which class of request, what happens when a provider degrades, and how you move between them without rewriting the product.

docs.title: Cost and latency budgets
docs.text: Tokens per unit of work, caching, batching and an agreed response-time target, so the feature is affordable at the volume you actually expect.

docs.title: It answers confidently from nothing
docs.text: No grounding, no citation, no refusal path. The fix is retrieval design and an explicit “I do not know”, not a sterner prompt.

docs.title: It answers from documents the user may not see
docs.text: Entitlements were applied to the application and not to the index. This is the failure that stops enterprise rollouts.

docs.title: It was right in the demonstration
docs.text: A handful of questions is not a test set. Without a graded golden set you have an anecdote with a launch date.

docs.title: It cost four times the estimate
docs.text: Context assembled without a budget, no caching, and a model chosen for the hardest request and used for all of them.

docs.title: What the integration involves
docs.text: The model is the smallest decision in this list. Everything else is what determines whether the feature is reliable, affordable and defensible.

docs.title: All of them are design problems, not model problems
docs.text: Every one of these is recoverable, and every one is considerably cheaper to prevent than to discover in front of a customer.

docs.title: What is RAG and when is it the right approach?
docs.text: Retrieval-augmented generation means the model answers from passages retrieved out of your own content at the time of the question, rather than from what it absorbed in training. It is the right approach when answers must reflect current, organisation-specific material and must be checkable against a source, which covers most enterprise knowledge use cases.

docs.title: Can you add AI to a product we already have?
docs.text: Yes, and it is one of the most common engagements. Model or agent capability is integrated into an existing application, knowledge base or workflow while preserving the systems, permissions and controls already in place, rather than requiring the product to be rebuilt around the feature.

docs.title: Can you build a chatbot for our business?
docs.text: Usually what is wanted is not a chatbot in the 2017 sense but an assistant that answers from your own documents, records and policies, respects who is allowed to see what, and cites the passage it answered from. That is retrieval work rather than conversation design, and it is what this page describes. Where the need genuinely is a scripted flow over a handful of known questions, a simpler tool is cheaper and we will say so rather than build a model into it.

docs.title: How do you stop a model answering from documents a user is not allowed to see?
docs.text: By modelling permissions before the index is built, so entitlements are enforced at retrieval rather than applied afterwards in the application layer. Retrieval that respects who is allowed to see what is the part of enterprise RAG that most often decides whether a rollout goes ahead.

docs.title: Assist, understand, act, discover
docs.text: AI is not only for email, meetings and documents. It can sit inside a product, a customer experience, an operation or a forecast, and what it does there tends to take one of four forms.

docs.title: Three ways AI is built into a business
docs.text: AI systems are how a product understands. Agents and automation are how it acts. Evaluation and observability is how you know it works. They overlap in practice, and a programme often needs two of them.

docs.title: Where AI earns its place
docs.text: Not by industry or company size, but by whether better context, reasoning, coordination or automation would materially change the outcome.

docs.title: How production AI works
docs.text: A model answers questions. A production system has to reach the right information, act inside its permissions, and still be right in six months.

docs.title: How do we know it actually works?
docs.text: Building it is only part of the job. You also need to know whether it works.

docs.title: Start with the problem, not the model
docs.text: We start with what you are trying to achieve, then work out whether AI is the right tool and how its success will be measured. Sometimes the answer is that it is not.

docs.title: What could AI do for my organisation?
docs.text: More than office administration. AI can assist with work already being done, understand text, speech, images and data that are slow to process by hand, act inside products and systems within defined permissions, and surface patterns, forecasts and anomalies that were hard to see. That applies to software products, customer and retail experiences, personal and wellbeing apps, operations and industrial settings as much as to back-office work. Whether AI is the right tool for a particular problem is the first thing a Value Discovery establishes.

docs.title: What is a Value Discovery?
docs.text: A four-week engagement. Two or three processes are instrumented and measured, the measurement is left running and is yours to keep, and you receive a prioritised opportunity map, a costed roadmap and a board-ready business case naming the budget line it displaces. If the numbers do not support going further, Pixelette says so in writing.

docs.title: Does Pixelette Technologies audit or certify the AI it builds?
docs.text: No, and it does not offer to. Where a programme needs formal governance, certification readiness, privacy or security-assurance support, Pixelette Certified, a separate practice in the same group, can scope the requirement, coordinate appropriately credentialed specialists and support the route to independent assessment. Independent assurance stays independent: the firm that builds a system is not the firm that assesses it.

docs.title: Predictive Intelligence
docs.text: Forecasting, scoring, recommendation and decision-support systems built around business data, with thresholds, monitoring and a decision they actually change.

docs.title: Forecasting
docs.text: Demand, revenue, capacity, cash and workload, at the horizon and granularity a decision is actually taken at rather than the one that produces the prettiest chart.

docs.title: Scoring and propensity
docs.text: Risk, churn, conversion likelihood, credit and priority, expressed as a score with a defined meaning and a defined action at each band.

docs.title: Recommendation and personalisation
docs.text: Next best action, product and content ranking, and the guardrails that stop a recommender optimising itself into a corner.

docs.title: Anomaly detection
docs.text: Finding the transaction, reading or record that does not belong, tuned to the alert volume a human team can genuinely investigate.

docs.title: Decision support
docs.text: The prediction placed inside the workflow where the decision happens, with the reasoning shown and the person still making the call.

docs.title: Monitoring for decay
docs.text: Models age as the world moves. Input drift, changing distributions and falling accuracy are watched continuously rather than noticed in a quarterly review.

docs.title: A decision that would change
docs.text: If the same action follows every prediction, the prediction is decoration. We ask this question first and it disqualifies a fair number of ideas.

docs.title: History with the outcome in it
docs.text: You cannot learn to predict something your records never recorded. What is missing is often the outcome, not the inputs.

docs.title: A threshold somebody owns
docs.text: A score becomes useful at the point where a person agrees what happens above and below a line, and accepts the cost of being wrong in each direction.

docs.title: An honest accuracy target
docs.text: Set against the current human baseline, not against zero. Beating nothing is not a result worth funding.

docs.title: Four conditions, checked in that order
docs.text: They take an afternoon to establish and they are the difference between a model in production and a notebook nobody opens.

docs.title: What is predictive intelligence used for?
docs.text: Forecasting demand, revenue, capacity or workload; scoring risk, churn, conversion or priority; recommendation and personalisation; anomaly detection; and decision support that puts the prediction inside the workflow where the decision is actually taken.

docs.title: What does a predictive project need before it can start?
docs.text: Four things: a decision that would genuinely change as a result, historical data that recorded the outcome and not only the inputs, a threshold somebody is willing to own, and an accuracy target set against the current human baseline rather than against zero. Where any of those is missing, we say so before scoping a build.

docs.title: How do you keep a model accurate after it goes live?
docs.text: By monitoring for decay as a standing commitment: input drift, changing distributions and falling accuracy against held-out outcomes, with an agreed threshold below which the model is retrained or withdrawn. A predictive system that nobody is watching becomes confidently wrong rather than obviously broken.

docs.title: When should a workflow use an AI agent, and when should it not?
docs.text: Use an agent when the path genuinely varies per case, the system must choose among tools, and a wrong step is recoverable and reviewable. Do not use one when the process is stable, the steps are known, the output is regulated, or nobody can articulate what "correct" looks like well enough to grade it.

docs.title: Are most "agentic" products actually agentic?
docs.text: No. 17% of organisations have deployed AI agents, over 40% of agentic projects are forecast to be cancelled by the end of 2027 on cost, unclear value or inadequate controls, and of the thousands of vendors claiming agentic capability Gartner assesses roughly 130 as genuinely agentic. Much of what is sold as agentic should be a deterministic workflow with one model call in it, which is cheaper, faster and auditable.

docs.text: Receiving, reading, extracting, validating and filing the material a process runs on, including the awkward formats nobody wants to admit are still in use.

docs.title: Human approval steps
docs.text: Approvals designed as part of the flow, with the right context put in front of the right person, rather than an email asking someone to go and look at something.

docs.title: Exception handling
docs.text: The cases that fall out of the happy path. An automation that handles eighty per cent and silently drops the rest has moved the work, not removed it.

docs.title: Reporting on what changed
docs.text: Volume processed, time saved, exceptions raised, and the same measurements taken before the automation existed, so the comparison is real.

docs.title: What kinds of process are worth automating?
docs.text: Repetitive or high-friction processes that cross several systems, involve documents or structured data, and have a measurable current cost in time, cycle time or error rate. Processes that run rarely, change constantly, or carry a decision nobody can define well enough to grade are usually poor candidates, and we will say so.

docs.title: Does workflow automation need AI?
docs.text: Frequently not. A large share of the value in a business process comes from deterministic integration and orchestration, which is cheaper to run and simpler to audit. A model is introduced where the work genuinely requires judgement, extraction or language handling that rules cannot do.

docs.title: How do you prove an automation was worth it?
docs.text: By measuring the process before it is changed. The manual cost, cycle time, error rate or conversion baseline is instrumented first, so afterwards the comparison is against a recorded starting point rather than against a recollection of how bad things used to be.

Blockchain Integration
docs.text: Connect blockchain components to existing applications, data and off-chain systems, including indexing, identity mapping, settlement and reconciliation.

docs.title: On-chain and off-chain boundary
docs.text: Deciding what genuinely belongs on a chain and what belongs in a database. Almost every workable design puts far less on-chain than the first proposal did.

docs.title: Indexing and read models
docs.text: Chain data is expensive and slow to query directly. An indexing layer turns it into something an application can read at product speed and a report can be built on.

docs.title: Identity and access mapping
docs.text: Connecting an address to a customer record, a permission set and an audit trail, so on-chain activity is attributable inside your own systems.

docs.title: Payments and settlement
docs.text: Where value moves between chain and conventional rails, with the states, retries, timeouts and failure paths designed rather than assumed.

docs.title: Reconciliation and reporting
docs.text: Making chain state, application state and finance records agree, and producing the evidence when they do not. Nobody enjoys this and everybody eventually needs it.

docs.title: Operational monitoring
docs.text: Node and provider health, confirmation depth, fee conditions, stuck transactions and reorganisations, alerting to people who can act on them.

docs.title: Finality is not instant
docs.text: A transaction that looks confirmed is a probability, not a fact. Applications that treat it as a fact eventually reverse a customer’s balance.

docs.title: Fees are a runtime condition
docs.text: Cost and confirmation time move with network conditions. A design that ignores this works beautifully until the week it does not.

docs.title: Bridges concentrate risk
docs.text: Cross-chain movement has been one of the most heavily exploited areas in the field. We treat a bridging requirement as a reason to re-examine the design.

docs.title: Providers are a dependency
docs.text: Node providers, indexers and price feeds are third parties with outages. They belong in your resilience plan alongside every other supplier.

docs.title: What the work covers
docs.text: Integration is where a blockchain project stops being a proof of concept and starts being something a business can operate.

docs.title: What does blockchain integration involve?
docs.text: Connecting on-chain components to the applications, data and off-chain systems a business already runs: deciding the boundary between chain and database, building the indexing layer that makes chain state readable at product speed, mapping addresses to customer records and permissions, handling settlement between chain and conventional rails, and reconciling chain state with application and finance records.

docs.title: Why do you need an indexing layer?
docs.text: Because querying a chain directly is slow and expensive, and applications and reports need data at product speed. An indexing layer reads chain events into a queryable read model, which is also what makes reconciliation, reporting and customer support practical.

docs.title: What are the main operational risks in integrating a chain?
docs.text: Treating apparent confirmation as final when it is probabilistic; designs that assume stable fees and confirmation times; cross-chain bridges, which have been among the most heavily exploited components in the field; and dependence on third-party node providers, indexers and price feeds that have outages like any other supplier.

docs.text: Both are the same problem: proving a system behaved correctly to somebody who assumes it did not. docs.title: Justification and requirement analysis
docs.text: Establishing what a general-purpose chain fails to provide for your case: throughput, cost, privacy, governance, finality or control. Without a specific failure, this work should not start.

docs.title: Consensus and validator design
docs.text: Who validates, how they are selected, what they are paid, what happens when they misbehave, and how the set changes over time.

docs.title: Execution and state
docs.text: The execution environment, state model, fee mechanism and the compatibility decisions that determine whether existing tooling works or has to be rebuilt.

docs.title: Scaling layers and rollups
docs.text: Where a Layer 2 answers the requirement without the burden of a sovereign network, including data availability, settlement and exit design.

docs.title: Node operations and upgrades
docs.text: Running a network is an operational commitment: releases, coordinated upgrades, observability, incident response and the governance to agree a change.

docs.title: Economic and incentive design
docs.text: Fees, rewards, issuance and the behaviour those incentives will actually produce, including the behaviour you did not intend.

docs.title: Name the failure
docs.text: Which specific requirement does an existing chain not meet? A general dissatisfaction is not a specification.

docs.title: Cost the operation
docs.text: A network needs validators, upgrades, monitoring and a team, indefinitely. That standing cost usually decides the question.

docs.title: Count the ecosystem
docs.text: A new network starts with no wallets, no explorers, no tooling and no integrations. Everything you assumed exists must be built.

docs.title: Exhaust the alternatives
docs.text: An app-specific chain, a rollup, a permissioned network or an existing chain with a different design frequently meet the same requirement for far less.

docs.title: Four tests before this work is worth starting
docs.text: Most enquiries that reach this page do not pass all four, and saying so is considerably more useful than taking the engagement.

docs.title: What the work covers
docs.text: Where the tests are passed, the engineering spans consensus, execution, operations and the incentives that hold the whole thing together.

docs.title: When is a bespoke chain or Layer 2 actually justified?
docs.text: When a general-purpose chain demonstrably fails a specific requirement: throughput, cost per transaction, privacy, governance, finality guarantees or control over upgrades, and the alternatives have been exhausted. Absent a named failure of that kind, an existing chain, an app-specific rollup or a permissioned network will usually meet the requirement for a fraction of the standing cost.

docs.title: What is the real cost of running your own network?
docs.text: It is an operational commitment rather than a project. Validators have to be run or recruited, releases and coordinated upgrades managed, the network monitored and incidents handled, and governance maintained to agree changes. A new network also starts with no wallets, explorers, tooling or integrations, so everything a mature ecosystem provides has to be built or funded.

docs.title: Do you work on Layer 2 and rollups as well as Layer 1?
docs.text: Yes, and a scaling layer is frequently the better answer. A rollup can deliver the throughput and cost characteristics a project needs while inheriting settlement and much of the surrounding ecosystem from an established chain, which removes most of the sovereignty burden of a bespoke Layer 1.

docs.title: Contract design and specification
docs.text: What the contract must do, what it must refuse to do, and what it must never allow, written down before anything is deployed. On-chain, ambiguity becomes permanent.

docs.title: Testing and invariant checking
docs.text: Unit and integration tests, property and invariant testing, and adversarial cases written by someone trying to break it. Testing is the deliverable, not the overhead.

docs.title: Access control and role design
docs.text: Who may call what, which roles exist, how they are granted and revoked, and what any single compromised key can actually do.

docs.title: Upgrade and ownership decisions
docs.text: Whether the contract can be changed after deployment, by whom, under what delay, and what the holder can do about it. A choice with real governance consequences, made explicitly.

docs.title: dApp front end and indexing
docs.text: The interface people use, the indexing layer that makes chain state readable at speed, and the transaction states that a wallet leaves you to explain.

docs.text: Documentation, specification, test evidence and code structured so an independent security firm can review it efficiently rather than starting from archaeology.

docs.title: What we do
docs.text: Design, write, test and document contracts, including adversarial testing and invariant checks, and structure the work so that independent review is efficient.

docs.title: What we do not claim
docs.text: We do not describe our own testing as an audit. An audit is a separate, independent engagement with its own competence, scope and liability.

docs.text: An independent security firm, engaged by you. A supplier reviewing its own contracts is not assurance, whatever the report is called.

docs.title: What you get from us
docs.text: The specification, the test suite and its results, the deployment and ownership plan, and remediation of findings the reviewer raises.

docs.title: We do not call our own testing an audit
docs.text: The word carries a specific meaning in this market and it is routinely misused. Here is exactly where the boundary sits on our engagements.

docs.title: Do you audit smart contracts?
docs.text: No, and we are careful with the word. We design, write, test and document contracts, including adversarial testing and invariant checks, and we structure the work so an independent security review can be carried out efficiently. An audit is a separate engagement by an independent firm with its own competence and scope, and a supplier reviewing its own contracts is not assurance.

docs.title: Should a smart contract be upgradeable?
docs.text: It is a governance decision rather than a technical default. Upgradeability lets defects be fixed, and also means someone can change the rules after people have committed value under them. The decision should be explicit, documented, constrained by delays or multi-party control where the stakes justify it, and visible to whoever is relying on the contract.

docs.title: What does a dApp involve beyond the contracts?
docs.text: An interface, an indexing layer that makes chain state readable at usable speed, wallet connection and transaction-state handling, off-chain services for anything that should not be on-chain, and monitoring. The contracts are typically the smallest component and the least forgiving one.

docs.title: Tokenisation
docs.text: Architecture and implementation for representing and managing real-world or digital assets on-chain, where the commercial and legal model genuinely supports it.

docs.title: Asset and rights modelling
docs.text: What the token actually represents: ownership, a claim, a right to a distribution, access, or a unit of account. Everything downstream is determined by this and it is a commercial and legal question before it is a technical one.

docs.title: Token standard and chain selection
docs.text: Fungible or non-fungible, transferable or restricted, and on which network. Chosen against the operating requirement rather than against whichever ecosystem is currently loudest.

docs.title: Issuance and lifecycle
docs.text: Minting, allocation, vesting, transfer restrictions, redemption and retirement. The end of a token’s life is designed at the beginning or it is not designed at all.

docs.title: Custody and key management
docs.text: Who holds the keys, under what controls, and what happens when a key is lost or a person leaves. The most common single point of failure in this category.

docs.title: Holder and investor interfaces
docs.text: The dashboards, statements, transaction views and administrative tooling through which people actually experience the thing. Usually the larger part of the build.

docs.title: Treasury and reporting visibility
docs.text: What the operator, the holder and the auditor can each see, and how an on-chain position reconciles to the off-chain records it is meant to correspond to.

docs.title: Who is the counterparty?
docs.text: A token represents a relationship with someone. If nobody is obliged to honour what it represents, the chain does not create the obligation.

docs.title: What is the legal wrapper?
docs.text: The commercial and legal structure comes first. Architecture built ahead of it usually has to be rebuilt around it.

docs.title: Who may hold it?
docs.text: Transfer restrictions, identity checks and jurisdiction shape the token design directly, and retrofitting them is expensive.

docs.title: Would a database do?
docs.text: If there is no shared record between separate parties, no independent verification requirement and no genuine need for programmable ownership, the honest answer is often yes.

docs.title: What the work covers
docs.text: From the rights model through to the interfaces holders and operators actually use, and the reporting that reconciles the two.

docs.title: Four questions we ask before quoting
docs.text: They are cheap to answer at the start and extremely expensive to answer after a token has been issued to real holders.

docs.title: What does Pixelette Technologies mean by tokenisation?
docs.text: Architecture and implementation for representing and managing real-world or digital assets on-chain, where the commercial and legal model supports it. That covers rights modelling, token standard and chain selection, issuance and lifecycle, custody, holder interfaces, and the reconciliation between on-chain positions and off-chain records.

docs.title: What has to be settled before a tokenisation build starts?
docs.text: What the token represents and who is obliged to honour it, the legal and commercial wrapper around it, who is permitted to hold and transfer it, and whether a conventional database would meet the requirement. Those four answers determine the architecture, and building ahead of them normally means rebuilding afterwards.

docs.title: Will you tell us if we do not need a blockchain?
docs.text: Yes. Blockchain is treated as a specialist tool rather than a default answer, and is used where ownership, programmability, verification, tokenisation or multi-party verification creates a genuine advantage. Where a conventional system would do the job, that is the recommendation, including when it is the smaller piece of work.

docs.title: Wallets & Digital-Asset Products
docs.text: User-facing wallet, portfolio and transaction experiences across mobile and web, designed around key management, recovery and irreversible actions.

docs.title: Custody model
docs.text: Custodial, non-custodial or multi-party. The choice determines your regulatory position, your support burden and what happens on the worst day, so it is decided first and deliberately.

docs.title: Key management and recovery
docs.text: Generation, storage, backup, rotation and the recovery route for a user who has lost a device. Recovery design is the difference between a product and a trap.

docs.title: Portfolio and transaction views
docs.text: Balances, history, valuations and statements that reconcile, presented so a person can understand their own position without a block explorer open beside it.

docs.title: Transaction safety
docs.text: Confirmation design, simulation, address verification, spending limits and approval flows. Most user losses are authorised by the user, which makes this an interface problem.

docs.title: Integration points
docs.text: On and off ramps, exchanges, price sources, identity checks and the accounting systems that eventually have to agree with what the wallet says.

docs.title: Mobile and web delivery
docs.text: Native iOS and Android and web interfaces, with secure local storage, biometrics and the device-level behaviour these products depend on.

docs.title: Irreversible actions need friction
docs.text: A transfer cannot be recalled. The interface should be hardest at exactly the moment a mistake becomes permanent.

docs.title: Recovery is a product feature
docs.text: Not a support process. Design it before launch, and design it for the least technical person who will hold the app.

docs.title: Show what will happen
docs.text: Simulate and state the outcome before signing, in ordinary language. Approval screens that nobody can read are consent in name only.

docs.title: The books have to agree
docs.text: Whatever the wallet shows must reconcile with the chain and with your finance records. Three versions of a balance is an incident waiting for an auditor.

docs.title: What is the difference between a custodial and a non-custodial wallet?
docs.text: In a custodial model the operator holds the keys and can act on the user’s behalf, which simplifies recovery and support but places the operator in a regulated position of responsibility. In a non-custodial model the user holds the keys, which removes that responsibility and removes the safety net with it. Multi-party approaches sit between the two. The choice is a risk and operating decision and should be made before the product is designed.

docs.title: What is the hardest part of building a wallet?
docs.text: Recovery and transaction safety, not the chain interaction. A wallet is a key-management system with a product interface on it: what happens when a user loses a device, and how clearly the interface communicates an irreversible action before it is signed, determine whether the product is safe to use.

docs.title: Can a wallet be part of a wider product rather than a standalone app?
docs.text: Yes, and frequently it should be. Wallet, portfolio and transaction functionality is often one surface of a larger financial or platform programme across mobile and web, with the digital-asset capability sitting alongside conventional account, reporting and administration features rather than in a separate application.

docs.title: What is the difference between cloud engineering and data engineering here?
docs.text: Cloud engineering is where the system runs: environments, deployment, observability, resilience and cost. docs.title: Native iOS and Android
docs.text: Where the product depends on platform behaviour, background work, hardware access or interface conventions that a shared codebase will fight rather than use.

docs.title: Cross-platform builds
docs.text: One codebase across both stores where the product is mostly screens, data and forms, and the saving is real rather than theoretical.

docs.title: Offline behaviour and sync
docs.text: What the app does on a train, in a basement or on a bad connection, and what happens to the data when the signal comes back.

docs.title: Device capability
docs.text: Camera, location, biometrics, notifications, background processing and secure local storage, with the permission prompts designed rather than defaulted.

docs.text: Review requirements, privacy declarations, staged rollout, versioning and the discipline of shipping to an audience that cannot be forced to update.

docs.title: The back end behind the app
docs.text: APIs, authentication, push infrastructure and integrations. A mobile app is a client; most of the engineering is usually behind it.

docs.title: Choose native when
docs.text: The product leans on platform behaviour, hardware, background execution or performance, or the interface has to feel genuinely at home on each platform.

docs.title: Choose cross-platform when
docs.text: The app is largely screens, data and forms, both platforms need parity, and one team maintaining one codebase is worth more than the last few per cent of native feel.

docs.title: Choose neither when
